title: 道德經 第三十二章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 32, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 68. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 32 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 聖德 (Sagely Potency). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
道常無名，
樸雖小，
天下莫能臣也。
侯王若能守之，
萬物將自賓。

morph.gloss: abidingly, always-so (adverb here, before the verb)
the uncarved block — timber as it left the tree, before any tool shaped it
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world, and everyone in it
no one, nothing — a negative that carries its own subject
to make a subject of, to hold as a vassal — the NOUN 'subject, minister' used as a verb
final particle: closes the statement as settled
the lords and kings — the rulers of states, named by their two ranks
a marquis, a lord holding land of the king
to guard, to keep, to hold on to
the ten thousand things — everything there is
would, are about to (jiāng, the adverb before the verb)
of themselves — the reflexive always stands before its verb
to act the guest, to submit as a guest does to his host — the NOUN 'guest' used as a verb

sentences.l:
The Way abidingly lacks a name.
The uncarved block, small though it is,
none under heaven can make a subject of.
If lords and kings could hold to it,
the ten-thousand things would of themselves come as guests.
sentences.i: The Way is nameless, and abidingly so. Small as the uncarved block is, no one under heaven can make a subject of it. If only lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would come of their own accord and give themselves up as guests.
sentences.n: Two nouns are working as verbs in these five lines, and they are the whole lesson. 臣 is 'a subject, a minister'; 天下莫能臣也 makes a verb of it — none can vassal it, hold it in subjection. 賓 is 'a guest'; 自賓 is 'of themselves play the guest', come in and submit as a guest submits to his host. Nothing on the page marks either change; only the position does. Note also that 莫 is a negative carrying its own subject — 'no one, nothing' — so the line needs no separate word for 'none'. This is one of the chapters the Guodian bamboo slips (c. 300 BC, the oldest witness we have) contain, and there, as in the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, 常 is written 恆 héng: the Han changed that character everywhere to avoid the personal name of Emperor Wen, and chapter 1 met the same swap. Wang Bi's comment sets the small thing against the unsubduable one: the uncarved block, he says, takes not-having for its heart and has no name either, and so if a man would get the Way there is nothing like keeping to the uncarved block.

sentences.t:
天地相合，
以降甘露，
民莫之令而自均。

morph.gloss: heaven and earth; the cosmos taken as a pair
one another, mutually — placed before the verb
to come together, to close upon each other, to be in accord
to send down, to let fall (jiàng; read xiáng it is 'to surrender')
sweet dew — the standing omen of a reign in right order, dew that falls of itself
the people, the common folk — the ruled, as against their ruler
them — the object, standing BEFORE its verb because the clause is negative
to order, to give commands to
even, level, evenly shared — of what has settled flat of its own weight

sentences.i: Heaven and earth come together, and the sweet dew falls; and the people, with no one giving them orders, settle of their own accord into evenness.
sentences.n: 莫之令 puts the object in front of the verb, and the rule behind it is one of the firmest in the language: in a negative clause a pronoun object goes before the verb it belongs to. So this is 'no one orders them', never 'no one is ordered'. You met the same shape in chapter 9's 莫之能守. 甘露 is not merely dew that tastes sweet: it is the standing omen of a reign in good order, the dew that comes down unasked when heaven and earth are in accord. Wang Bi joins the two halves of the unit at exactly that point — when heaven and earth are joined, the sweet dew is not sought and descends of itself; and if I keep to my true nature and act without forcing, the people are not commanded and come out even of themselves. 均 is evenness that has settled, not evenness that has been arranged.

sentences.t:
始制有名，
名亦既有，
夫亦將知止，
知止所以不殆。

morph.gloss: properly to cut cloth to a pattern — hence to shape, to regulate, to institute
already — marks the thing as accomplished, 'once they are there'
now — the opening particle (fú), resuming after the condition
is going to, is to (jiāng, the adverb before the verb)
to stop, to come to rest; where to halt
that whereby, the means by which — not the modern Mandarin 'therefore'
to come to harm, to be brought into danger

sentences.l:
Once the cutting-out begins, there are names;
and names being already there,
one must also know where to stop.
Knowing where to stop is that whereby one comes to no harm.
sentences.i: Once the shaping begins there are names; and the names being there now, a man must know as well where to stop. Knowing where to stop is what keeps him out of harm.
sentences.n: Wang Bi reads 始制 as the moment chapter 28 described: the uncarved block broken up, and officers set over the pieces (樸散則為器 … 則為官長). That is why 制 is the right character for it — properly the tailor's cut, cloth shaped to a pattern, hence to regulate and to institute — and why names follow at once: ranks once made must be named to be told apart. And then, Wang Bi warns, men press on past that point and end by fighting over the tip of an awl; hence 'know where to stop'. 所以 is the fixed pair met in chapter 7's 天地所以能長且久者 — 'that whereby', the means by which. 既 marks a thing already accomplished. 將 is properly 'is going to'; reading it here as something nearer an obligation — this is what one is to do — is an interpretation the sense invites, not something the character itself states.

sentences.t:
譬道之在天下，
猶川谷之於江海。

morph.gloss: to compare, to put it by way of illustration
— here 之 stands between subject and verb and makes the whole clause a noun
to be in, to be present in
a stream, a watercourse — with 谷 following, the streams that run in the valleys
a valley, a ravine — the empty low place into which everything runs
again between subject and verb, making a noun of the clause: 'the valley streams' standing-toward ——'
the great river — properly the Yangtze, as 河 is the Yellow River

sentences.l:
To compare: the Way's being in all-under-heaven
is like the valley streams' being toward the great rivers and the sea.
sentences.i: Put it this way: the Way stands to all under heaven as the streams of the valleys stand to the great rivers and the sea.
sentences.n: 之 is doing a third job here, and it is the one most easily missed. Set between a subject and its verb it makes the whole clause into a noun: 道之在天下 is not a sentence, 'the Way is in all under heaven', but a thing, 'the-Way's-being-in-all-under-heaven' — which is what a comparison needs, since you cannot compare two sentences, only two things. Genitive, object pronoun, and now this: one character, three jobs, and only position to tell them apart. Wang Bi puts the weight of the comparison on which way the water runs: the valley streams do not go to the rivers and the sea because the rivers and the sea have called them — uncalled and unasked, they return there of themselves.
